t: Estrogen alone, or a progestogen added?
key: Ask whether an endometrium is still there. Estrogen alone lets the lining grow unopposed into hyperplasia and cancer, so any woman with a uterus on systemic estrogen needs a progestogen, and only a woman without a uterus takes estrogen alone. The one exception is low-dose vaginal estrogen, which is barely absorbed.
items: Hot flashes after a total hysterectomy for fibroids
a
With no uterus there is no endometrium to overgrow, so a progestogen would add risk and side effects without any benefit.
Hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy at age 42
a
Both the ovaries and the uterus are gone, so estrogen alone replaces what is missing, and it is usually continued until about the age of natural menopause.
Women's Health Initiative arm that did not raise breast cancer
a
The estrogen-alone arm enrolled women after hysterectomy and did not increase breast cancer, although stroke and clot risk still rose; adding medroxyprogesterone is what raised breast cancer.
Daily estradiol patch for a woman whose uterus was removed
a
The route changes liver exposure and clot risk, not endometrial protection, so with the uterus gone the patch needs no progestogen partner.
Estrogen given with no endometrium left to overgrow
a
Hyperplasia and endometrial cancer arise when estrogen acts unopposed on the lining; after hysterectomy that target is gone, so unopposed estrogen carries no such risk.
Low-dose vaginal estrogen for dryness alone, even with an intact uterus
a
Very little is absorbed into the circulation, so the lining is not meaningfully stimulated and no progestogen is needed; this is the exception to the uterus rule.
Severe hot flashes at 52 with an intact uterus
b
Systemic estrogen would stimulate the endometrium unopposed, so a progestogen is added to keep the lining thin and prevent hyperplasia and cancer.
Cyclic regimen with a monthly withdrawal bleed
b
The progestogen is given for 12 to 14 days each month, which matures the lining and sheds it on schedule, so a planned bleed follows.
Continuous combined regimen that aims for no bleeding
b
Daily estrogen with daily progestogen keeps the lining thin and atrophic, so spotting is common at first and then usually stops.
Women's Health Initiative arm that raised breast cancer, stroke and clots
b

The combined arm gave conjugated estrogen with medroxyprogesterone to women who had a uterus, and it stopped early in 2002 because breast cancer, stroke, venous thromboembolism and coronary events rose.
Primary ovarian insufficiency at age 32 with a uterus
b
She needs estrogen until about age 51, and her uterus means a progestogen must protect the lining; the risks measured in older women in the Women's Health Initiative do not apply to her.
Micronized progesterone taken together with estradiol
b
Micronized progesterone is one way to supply the progestogen that opposes estrogen at the endometrium, alongside medroxyprogesterone, in a woman who still has a uterus.
